chain: Mild abrasive plaque and stain removal
baking-soda-toothpaste.text: Users pick baking soda toothpaste for a cleaner feel, lighter surface stain and fresher breath ahead of a better smile. Research on it centres on plaque and gum health, and whitening evidence is thinner.

chain: Plaque and calculus removed below gumline
Healthier, firmer gums and fresher breath
dentist-deep-cleaning-scaling-and-root-p.text: People get scaling and root planing to treat gum disease, which brings calmer, less swollen gums and less gum-related breath odour, and protects the teeth that frame the smile. It is a standard, well-studied periodontal treatment; cosmetic gains are a by-product of the disease treatment.

chain: Teeth kept, smile and breath preserved
periodontal-treatment.text: Periodontal treatment covers the care used to keep gums healthy and teeth in place, which underpins a stable smile line and fresher breath. It is well studied for gum disease itself; appearance outcomes are a downstream benefit.

chain: Even gumline and less tooth length
gum-grafting.text: People get gum grafts to cover exposed roots and restore an even, fuller gumline, so teeth look shorter and the smile frame looks more balanced. The covered root is a visible result of the surgery, and outcomes by technique are well studied.

chain: Gum tissue loosened through small hole
Receded gums covered without a graft
pinhole-surgical-technique-gum-recession.text: The pinhole technique is used to move gum back over exposed roots without taking tissue from the palate, giving a more even gumline. The coverage is visible after surgery; evidence is mainly small studies with limited long-term follow-up.

gum-recession-treatment.text: People treat gum recession, mostly with grafts, to cover exposed roots and bring back an even gumline, so teeth look natural in length. The visible coverage is the result of the procedure; techniques are widely studied and outcomes vary.

chain: Less gum showing in a smile
gingivectomy.text: Gingivectomy is used to reshape gum tissue, notably to reduce a gummy smile or remove overgrown gums so more of the tooth shows. The change is visible straight after healing, and the procedure is long established in dentistry.

tonsil-stone-removal.text: People clear tonsil stones, by rinsing, gentle removal or clinic treatment, to cut a recognised source of bad breath. The stone-breath link is documented mostly in case reports and reviews rather than trials.

tonsillectomy.text: In looksmaxxing discussions tonsillectomy comes up as a last-resort option for severe, recurring tonsil stones and the breath odour they cause. Guidelines support it for recurrent infection and sleep apnoea; its use for stones is based on anecdote and case reports.

treating-gerd-for-breath.text: Users manage reflux in the hope of clearing a sour or acidic breath. Reflux is listed as a possible contributor to bad breath, though many researchers see the stomach as an uncommon source and trials on breath outcomes are limited.

treating-sinus-infection-for-breath.text: People treat sinusitis and post-nasal drip to remove a nasal source of breath odour. Nasal sources are recognised in principle, but breath-analysis trials testing this link have not been done.

h-pylori-treatment.text: Some people pursue H. pylori eradication hoping to improve persistent bad breath. Treatment is well established for ulcers and gastric cancer prevention, while its effect on breath has not been shown in trials.

chain: Ketone and protein by-products in breath
carnivore-diet-breath.text: Carnivore dieters report changes in breath odour and discuss it as a grooming and social concern alongside ketogenic eating. The pattern rests on anecdote; no studies look at carnivore breath specifically.

cutting-sugar-for-gums.text: People cut sugar to reduce plaque and support gum health, with cleaner teeth and calmer gums as the goal. Sugar's link to cavities is well studied, while gum-specific trials were not found.

vitamin-c-for-gums.text: Vitamin C is taken for gum health, given that deficiency (scurvy) causes bleeding gums. Dental trials on gum pigmentation treatment are ongoing, with little published, and benefits beyond correcting deficiency are untested.

coq10-for-gums.text: CoQ10 is taken or applied as an add-on to reduce gum inflammation in periodontitis. Trials are registered, but published results were not found.

chain: Vitamins D and K2 support mineralisation
vitamin-d-and-k2-for-teeth.text: Folk claims hold that vitamins D and K2 help teeth remineralise and rebuild. The rationale borrows from bone research, where K2 aids mineral formation; dental trials of the idea have not been run.

chain: Early damage and white spots repaired
remineralising-toothpaste.text: Users choose fluoride, nano-hydroxyapatite and similar pastes to repair early enamel damage and keep teeth smooth and strong. Fluoride has the strongest evidence for remineralisation, with newer agents less studied.

ozone-therapy-for-gums.text: Ozone gas, water or oil is promoted as a way to kill gum-disease bacteria without antibiotics. The gum benefit is a claim from alternative dentistry; ozone therapy broadly is unproven and the FDA reports no demonstrated safe medical use.

pulling-coconut-oil-for-gums.text: Oil pulling comes from Ayurvedic practice and is used for gum health and a cleaner-feeling mouth. The ADA reports no reliable studies supporting it, while the Canadian Dental Association does not expect harm.

hydrogen-peroxide-gum-rinse.text: Diluted peroxide is swished as a gum antiseptic to calm gingivitis. Some trials support a benefit for gingivitis, though chlorhexidine is reported to be more effective.

chain: Better plaque control and circulation claimed
gum-massage-stillman-technique.text: The Stillman technique and gum massage are discussed online as ways to improve gum health along the gumline. Little supporting evidence was found in the sources reviewed.

dry-mouth-management-biotene.text: Saliva substitutes such as Biotene are used to relieve dry mouth, which is tied to stale breath. They give short-term relief; no topical therapy has strong evidence.

drinking-water-frequently.text: Frequent water sipping is a common suggestion in breath-care guides for dry mouth and mouth odour. It is a low-cost habit, and trial evidence on its effect on odour was not found.

chain: Smoke odour and gum damage reduced
quit-smoking-and-vaping-for-breath.text: Looksmaxxers quit smoking and vaping to lose smoke odour on the breath and protect the gums, as a low-cost grooming change. The gum-health link is well documented, while appearance-specific trials have not been done.

retainer-and-mouthguard-cleaning.text: Grooming-minded users clean retainers and mouthguards to avoid bacterial buildup and odour. The idea is plausible by analogy with denture hygiene, with little direct study.

laser-iris-depigmentation-stroma-laser.text: Hardmaxxing communities discuss it as a way to lighten brown eyes without an implant. Reference summaries say it is not approved for cosmetic use and no trials were found.

chain: Silicone iris placed in the eye
newcoloriris-cosmetic-implants.text: These implants were placed in healthy eyes to change eye colour, with the new colour visible once in place. Published case series report serious complications, and the brand is described as no longer in use.

hypnosis-for-eye-color-change.text: Fringe corners of appearance culture claim hypnosis or suggestion recordings can alter iris colour. No studies have tested it, and reference sources report no evidence that hypnosis changes physical traits.

honey-drops-in-eyes.text: A folk claim in eye-colour discussions says diluted honey lightens the iris. It is untested and not an established cosmetic procedure, and ophthalmologists advise against related lightening drops.
